backchannels.direction: Ward's counts put yeah, uh-huh and okay at the top; a flat mm or clipped sure can brush the other person off.

reactions.direction: Friends may say you're kidding; with strangers a softer oh really is safer. Then give the floor back.

examples.text: Oh no, I'm sorry to hear that.

cant_hear.direction: Callers usually name the problem — you're breaking up, the line is bad — rather than stalling the talk to move rooms.

examples.text: Sorry, I can't hear you very well.
The line is bad on my side.
Could you speak a little louder?
I didn't catch that last part.

ask_repeat.direction: Sorry, could you say that again is the unmarked polite form; come again belongs with people you already know.

examples.text: Sorry, could you say that again?
Could you say the number again? It's 12345678?

who_is_calling.direction: Cambridge places who's calling after a request for someone; on a shared handset, say it is {owner}'s phone first.

examples.text: Hi, this is {owner}'s phone — who's calling?

wrong_number.direction: BBC models a brief sorry, you've got the wrong number and a goodbye, without asking how the number was found.

examples.text: Sorry, you've got the wrong number.
I think you must have the wrong number.
There's no one of that name here.

relay.direction: I'll pass that on or I'll let {owner} know finishes the job; give a callback time only if you can set it up.

examples.text: I'll pass that on to them.
I'll make sure they get the message.
I can tell her you called.
I'll pass your message on to him.

sales_decline.direction: No thanks, I'm not interested is the stock UK and US refusal; adding a reason can sound like negotiation.

examples.text: No thank you, I'm not interested.
Thanks, but we don't need that.
No thanks, please take us off your list.

firm_no.direction: The second English no is usually the same sentence, slowed down, plus please don't call again, still without abuse.

examples.text: I've already said no, please don't call again.
I'm not interested, and I need you to stop calling this number.
This is a final no — do not contact us again.

address_forms.direction: English has no T–V pronoun. First names with familiars; Mr, Ms or Dr plus surname; sir or madam with strangers.

avoid_service_phrases.direction: Helpline stock such as your call is important to us or how may I assist you today sounds corporate on a home line.

examples.text: Your call is important to us.
How may I assist you today?
It's my pleasure to be of service.
Thank you for calling {owner}'s office, your satisfaction is our priority.
Is there anything else I can help you with today?

taboo_on_phone.direction: Asking about marriage or pay in the first minutes, secret recording, or demanding ID all read as intrusive.

examples.text: Are you married? What's your salary?
Why hasn't {owner} called me back? Tell me where they are right now.
I'm recording this, just so you know — actually I already started.
Give me your address and ID number first.

uncertain: 美式與英式、澳紐用法在附和詞（right/okay/cheers）與稱呼（sir 較英式）上有差異，這裡以通用英語為主，不指定單一國家。
私人電話裡『How can I help you?』在熟人通話中會顯得像客服，但在代接、工作電話中仍常見；界線依場合而定。
『I’ll let them know』是否用於不認識的第三者，各地習慣不一，未找到單一語料頻率。
